title: Rising Public Revenue Fuels France's Rising Deficit - What's Next?
text:
Moroccan public finances in Q1 2026 posted a paradox: tax revenue surged 12.3% year-over-year to MAD 118.5 billion , yet the budget deficit widened to MAD 45.2 billion —a 28% increase from the same period last year—according to the latest Libération report , citing Treasury data. The divergence stems from a 15% spike in public spending on infrastructure and subsidies, outpacing revenue growth while inflation eroded fiscal buffers.
Why Did Revenue Rise While the Deficit Expanded? Three forces collided in Q1: a corporate tax windfall from mining and tourism sectors (up 22% YoY), but offset by lower-than-expected VAT collections due to delayed SME filings. Meanwhile, the government’s IMF-backed spending push —prioritizing renewable energy projects and agricultural subsidies—absorbed the gains.
View this post on Instagram about Karim Benjelloun, African Investment Bank From Instagram — related to Karim Benjelloun, African Investment Bank “The deficit isn’t a crisis—it’s a deliberate trade-off. Morocco’s fiscal strategy now hinges on whether the private sector can absorb the infrastructure investment gap.”
— Karim Benjelloun , CEO of African Investment Bank , in a Reuters interview (June 10, 2026) How the Fiscal Math Unfolded: A Quarter-by-Quarter Breakdown Metric Q1 2025 Q1 2026 YoY Change Source Total Revenue MAD 103.2bn MAD 118.5bn +12.3% Moroccan Treasury Tax Revenue MAD 89.7bn MAD 101.2bn +12.8% Libération Non-Tax Revenue MAD 13.5bn MAD 17.3bn +28.1% IMF Country Report Total Expenditure MAD 148.4bn MAD 163.7bn +10.3% Moroccan Treasury Deficit MAD 35.2bn MAD 45.2bn +28.4% Libération The revenue growth masks a structural issue: Morocco’s tax-to-GDP ratio remains below 20% , among the lowest in North Africa. While the mining sector (phosphates, rare earths) contributed MAD 18.7bn in Q1—up from MAD 15.2bn last year—the government’s subsidy bill for bread and fuel rose 35% YoY to MAD 22.1bn, per World Bank data . This crowding-out effect forces treasury officials to prioritize short-term social stability over long-term fiscal consolidation.
What Happens Next: The Private Sector’s Dilemma The widening deficit creates a liquidity crunch for Moroccan corporates , particularly in three sectors:
Morocco raises health and education spending in 2026 draft budget Infrastructure contractors reliant on government tenders now face delayed payments, with 30% of SMEs in the sector reporting cash-flow strain (per a Confédération Générale des Entreprises du Maroc (CGEM) survey ). Firms like Omnium Nord Africa are turning to specialized working capital providers to bridge gaps. Renewable energy developers —key beneficiaries of the government’s green investment push—are scrambling for project finance as state guarantees tighten. The Moroccan Agency for Sustainable Energy (MASEN) has already delayed three solar tenders due to budget reallocations, forcing firms to seek project finance advisory to restructure deals. Agribusinesses dependent on subsidized inputs now confront input cost inflation outpacing farmgate prices. The Office National de l’Electricité et de l’Eau Potable (ONEE) has warned of water rationing risks in key regions, pushing producers toward supply-chain risk management tools . The B2B Response: Who’s Filling the Gap? As the state’s fiscal flexibility shrinks, Moroccan businesses are turning to private-sector solutions to mitigate the fallout:
Corporate treasury firms like Standard Chartered’s Casablanca branch are seeing a 40% surge in demand for FX hedging as companies lock in rates amid currency volatility. “The dirham’s 2.5% depreciation against the euro this year has forced importers to act preemptively,” notes Leila El Moussawi , head of treasury services at the bank. Legal and compliance boutiques , such as Clifford Chance’s Casablanca office , are advising on public-private partnership (PPP) restructuring as local governments struggle to meet infrastructure obligations. “The window for renegotiating PPP contracts is now,” says Youssef Benali , partner at the firm. ESG-focused investors are stepping in where state funds fall short. The African Green Investment Bank has earmarked €500 million for Moroccan renewable projects, but only after securing local counterparty guarantees —a process now requiring specialized guarantee structuring expertise. What’s the Outlook for H2 2026? The Treasury’s mid-year review (due July 15) will test whether the government can rebalance spending without triggering a credit rating downgrade. Moody’s has already flagged Morocco’s F2 stable outlook as “under pressure” if the deficit exceeds 4.5% of GDP by year-end—a threshold the current trajectory risks breaching.
The private sector’s adaptability will determine whether this fiscal strain becomes a growth catalyst or a drag . Companies that fail to hedge currency risks, renegotiate PPP terms, or secure alternative financing will face margin compression in H2. Those that act swiftly—by leveraging corporate finance advisory , tax structuring , or supply-chain finance —will emerge as the quarter’s winners.
